text: Mide, also Meath, was a geographical division and a hero in ancient Ireland. Ancient Ireland had four provinces: Leinster in the east, Munster in the southwest, Connacht in the west, and Ulster in the northeast. There was also a fifth province, Mide or Meath, that was not of this world. It was a mysterious center point. This matches the Indo-European view of a world of four physical districts with an invisible center as the fifth. The name Mide means neck as well as middle. It was the point where the idea of the land's sovereignty, symbolized by the head, joined the physical land, symbolized by the body. That joining was said to happen on the hill of Uisneach, at the Stone of Divisions, now in County Westmeath. Mide was also a person, a druid and the son of Brath. He was fostered by the land goddess Ériu and lit the first fire on or near Uisneach. The fire blazed for seven years, fed by gifts from all of Ireland's provinces. In the seventh year other druids objected. Mide cut out their tongues and buried them in the hill. Then the woman druid Gaine named the place Uisneach, meaning over somewhat. After the reign of the high king Tuathal Teachmhair, about 130 to 160 C.E., a county at the center took the name Meath. It is still called royal Meath because the hill of Tara stood within it.

okr.objective: Document Mide, the fifth province and the druid of Uisneach.
